name: Vitamins and supplements: who may need them
summary: The NHS says most people can get what they need from a balanced diet, with vitamin D in autumn and winter and folic acid in early pregnancy as main exceptions.
keyPoints: NHS pages advise that everyone should consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter, because it is hard to get enough from food alone.
Some groups, including people who are rarely outdoors and people with dark skin, are advised to take vitamin D all year.
The NHS advises anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant to take a folic acid supplement until the twelfth week of pregnancy.
More is not always better: the NHS warns that very high vitamin D intakes could be harmful.

body.heading: Can a balanced diet provide everything?
body.body: NHS pages on vitamins and minerals describe getting what the body needs from a balanced diet, with supplements recommended only for some people and times of year. Vitamin D is the main example, because it is difficult for people to get enough from food alone.

body.heading: Who is advised to take vitamin D?
body.body: The NHS says everyone should consider a daily 10 microgram vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. NHS England starts this seasonal advice at age 4, while NHS inform in Scotland starts it at age 5. Some groups are advised to take it all year: people who are not often outdoors, such as those who are frail or housebound or living in care homes, people who usually cover most of their skin outdoors, and people with dark skin from African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds. For breastfed babies the NHS advises a daily vitamin D supplement throughout the year, and children aged 1 to 4 are also advised to take it year-round. Healthy Start vitamin products are free for eligible families.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about pregnancy?
body.body: Anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant is advised to take a 400 microgram folic acid supplement every day until the twelfth week of pregnancy. The NHS says some people need a higher dose, for example those with diabetes or taking medicine for epilepsy, and that this is arranged with a doctor.

body.heading: Can too much be harmful?
body.body: For vitamin D, the NHS says taking more than 100 micrograms a day could be harmful, and this applies to adults, pregnant and breastfeeding women and children aged 11 to 17. For folic acid, the NHS says too much could be harmful, but 1 milligram or less a day is unlikely to cause any harm.

body.heading: What do some common nutrients do?
body.body: The NHS guide to vitamins and minerals covers vitamins A, B, C, D, E and K, folic acid, calcium, iodine and iron. For vitamin A and for iron, the NHS says most people can get all they need from a varied and balanced diet. The NHS says vitamin D helps regulate the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body, and that sunlight is the main source. It says that from about late March or early April to the end of September most people can make all the vitamin D they need from sunlight on the skin. Iron is important for making red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body. Liver is very rich in vitamin A, and the NHS says liver or liver products such as pâté should not be eaten more than once a week.

headline: Vitamins and supplements: who the NHS says may need them
